. 2015-03-01 00:00:00 Abstract The prevalence of HIV infection in the United States has remained relatively stable over the past 5–10 years.
The prevalence of HIV and HCV coinfection is increasing, with the highest prevalence in the United States and Europe.
In summary, our research is concerned with
HIV and HCV co-infection, and with the clinical management of patients with HIV infection and HCV co- infection.
the study of hepatitis B and C virus (HBV and HCV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) co-infection in the context of antiretroviral therapy (ART).
understanding and improving the care for patients coinfected with HIV and HCV.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV/HCV coinfected patients are more likely to have more advanced liver disease and to develop HCC than HCV mono infected patients, with the risk being even greater if the patient has cirrhosis.

the HIV/HCV co-infected patient has a more rapid progression of liver disease, a higher risk of hepatocellular carcinoma, a higher rate of fibrosis and cirrhosis, and higher risk for death from liver disease.
HIV and HCV coinfection is a complex condition, with a wide variety of clinical manifestations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIV and HCV co-infected patients have worse outcomes than those who are infected with only one of these viruses.

we are now in a situation in which HIV and HCV co-infection is no longer a disease of the future, but rather a disease of today, which is characterized by a complex interaction between HIV and HCV infection.
we have been working in the field of HIV/HCV co-infection for more than 20 years.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have to think about HIV in the context of the hepatitis C virus (HCV) coinfection.
the HIV/HCV coinfected patient is now the patient who is older and more likely to have comorbidities.
we have a lot more to learn about the natural history of HIV and HCV coinfection.
